claim: Male mandarin voles after pair bonding released higher levels of DA in the NAc shell upon sniffing their partners compared to upon sniffing an unknown female.
source: This work verified that male mandarin voles after pair bonding released higher levels of DA in the NAc shell and displayed higher levels of D1 MSNs activity and lower levels of D2 MSNs activity upon sniffing their partners compared to upon sniffing an unknown female.
evidence: Supported by fiber photometry data showing DA release measurements in the NAc shell during social interactions (Figure 1G-I).

claim: Male mandarin voles after pair bonding displayed higher levels of D1 MSNs activity upon sniffing their partners compared to upon sniffing an unknown female.
source: This work verified that male mandarin voles after pair bonding released higher levels of DA in the NAc shell and displayed higher levels of D1 MSNs activity and lower levels of D2 MSNs activity upon sniffing their partners compared to upon sniffing an unknown female.
evidence: Supported by fiber photometry recordings of D1 MSNs calcium signals (Figure 3G-I).

claim: Male mandarin voles after pair bonding displayed lower levels of D2 MSNs activity upon sniffing their partners compared to upon sniffing an unknown female.
source: This work verified that male mandarin voles after pair bonding released higher levels of DA in the NAc shell and displayed higher levels of D1 MSNs activity and lower levels of D2 MSNs activity upon sniffing their partners compared to upon sniffing an unknown female.
evidence: Supported by fiber photometry recordings of D2 MSNs calcium signals (Figure 2G-I).

claim: Pair bonding induced differential alterations in synaptic plasticity in both D1 MSNs and D2 MSNs.
source: Moreover, pair bonding induced differential alterations in both synaptic plasticity and neuronal intrinsic excitability in both D1 MSNs and D2 MSNs.
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recordings showing changes in sEPSC and sIPSC frequencies and amplitudes (Figures 4 and 5).

claim: Pair bonding induced differential alterations in neuronal intrinsic excitability in both D1 MSNs and D2 MSNs.
source: Moreover, pair bonding induced differential alterations in both synaptic plasticity and neuronal intrinsic excitability in both D1 MSNs and D2 MSNs.
evidence: Supported by current-clamp recordings showing changes in action potential firing patterns (Figures 4E-H and 5E-H).

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of VP-projecting D2 MSNs in the NAc shell enhanced pair bond formation.
source: In addition, chemogenetic inhibition of ventral pallidum (VP) -projecting D2 MSNs in the NAc shell enhanced pair bond formation, while chemogenetic activation of VP-projecting D2 MSNs in the NAc shell inhibited pair bond formation.
evidence: Supported by partner preference test results following chemogenetic manipulation (Figure 6E and G).

claim: Chemogenetic activation of VP-projecting D2 MSNs in the NAc shell inhibited pair bond formation.
source: In addition, chemogenetic inhibition of ventral pallidum (VP) -projecting D2 MSNs in the NAc shell enhanced pair bond formation, while chemogenetic activation of VP-projecting D2 MSNs in the NAc shell inhibited pair bond formation.
evidence: Supported by partner preference test results following chemogenetic manipulation (Figure 6I and J).

claim: In monogamous animals, pair bonding is a selective, lasting relationship between two adult individuals forming a breeding pair.

evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Bales et al., 2021; López-Gutiérrez et al., 2021).

claim: Pair bonding is promoted by enduring social attraction between partners.

claim: Fluorescence signals were found to have increased in the NAc shell relative to baseline after cohabitation for 3 days when male voles sniffed either their partner or an unknown female.
source: Fluorescence signals were found to have increased in the NAc shell relative to baseline after cohabitation for 3 days when male voles sniffed either their partner or an unknown female (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A; Paired t test: partner, t (6)=3.290, p=0.0166; stranger, t (6)=4.884, p=0.0028; object, t (6)=1.745, p=0.1315).
evidence: Supported by fiber photometry data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A.

claim: Signal intensities showed no difference between sniffing their partner or an unknown female after three days cohabitation.
source: Signal intensities showed no difference between sniffing their partner or an unknown female after three days cohabitation (Figure 1D–F; One-Way Repeated Measures ANOVA: F (2.000, 12.00)=8.702, p=0.0001; partner vs. object, p=0.0060; stranger vs. object, p=0.0239).
evidence: Supported by fiber photometry data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1D-F.

claim: After cohabitation for 7 days, the extracellular DA concentration increased relative to baseline upon sniffing their partner or an unknown female.
source: However, after cohabitation for 7 days, although the extracellular DA concentration increased relative to baseline upon sniffing their partner or an unknown female (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B; Paired t test: partner, t (6)=6.020, p=0.0009; stranger, t (6)=2.611, p=0.0401; object, t (6)=2.209, p=0.0692), the extracellular DA concentration was significantly higher upon sniffing their partner than a stranger (Figure 1G–I; One-Way Repeated Measures ANOVA: F (2.000, 12.00) = 21.41, p=0.0002; partner vs. stranger, p=0.0097; partner vs. object, p<0.0001, stranger vs. object, p=0.0422).
evidence: Supported by fiber photometry data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5B and Figure 1G-I.

claim: After cohabitation for 7 days, the extracellular DA concentration was significantly higher upon sniffing their partner than a stranger.
source: However, after cohabitation for 7 days, although the extracellular DA concentration increased relative to baseline upon sniffing their partner or an unknown female (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B; Paired t test: partner, t (6)=6.020, p=0.0009; stranger, t (6)=2.611, p=0.0401; object, t (6)=2.209, p=0.0692), the extracellular DA concentration was significantly higher upon sniffing their partner than a stranger (Figure 1G–I; One-Way Repeated Measures ANOVA: F (2.000, 12.00) = 21.41, p=0.0002; partner vs. stranger, p=0.0097; partner vs. object, p<0.0001, stranger vs. object, p=0.0422).
evidence: Supported by fiber photometry data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1G-I.

claim: DA release in the NAc shell increased relative to baseline after cohabitation for 3 and 7 days when male voles sniffed an unknown male vole.
source: DA release in the NAc shell increased relative to baseline after cohabitation for 3 and 7 days when male voles sniffed an unknown male vole (Figure 1—figure supplement 6A and B; A, Paired t test: partner, t (5)=1.464, p=0.2030; stranger, t (5)=3.327, p=0.0209; object, t (5)=1.249, p=0.2669. evidence: Supported by fiber photometry data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6A and B.

claim: No difference was found in signal intensities between sniffing same-sex cagemates and unknown males.
source: DA release in the NAc shell increased relative to baseline after cohabitation for 3 and 7 days when male voles sniffed an unknown male vole (Figure 1—figure supplement 6A and B; A, Paired t test: partner, t (5)=1.464, p=0.2030; stranger, t (5)=3.327, p=0.0209; object, t (5)=1.249, p=0.2669. evidence: Supported by fiber photometry data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4D-I.

claim: When voles eat carrots, DA release increases in the NAc shell.

evidence: This is stated as an observation from the study.

claim: The fluorescence signal in the NAc shell increased upon eating carrot.
source: The results showed that the fluorescence signal in the NAc shell increased upon eating carrot (Figure 1—figure supplement 7B–D; Two-Way Repeated Measures ANOVA: group ×treatment: F (1, 7)=0.0274, p=0.8732; group: F (1, 7)=0.0557, p=0.8201; treatment: F (1, 7)=32.79, p=0.0007), but no significant difference in fluorescence signal was found while eating carrot between voles that had cohabitated for 3 and 7 days.

claim: No significant difference in fluorescence signal was found while eating carrot between voles that had cohabitated for 3 and 7 days.

claim: No significant differences were found between the fluorescence signals of DA release upon side-by-side contact with their partner and a stranger after 3 days of cohabitation.

claim: The fluorescence signals of DA release upon side-by-side contact with their partner were higher than that during the same behavior with a stranger after 7 days of cohabitation.

D, Paired t test: partner, t (6)=3.792, p=0.0091; stranger, t (6)=3.935, p=0.0077; object, t (6)=0.1841, p=0.8600).

claim: After 7 days of cohabitation, D2 MSNs activity when sniffing their partner was significantly lower than when sniffing a stranger.
source: In contrast, after 7 days of cohabitation, the activity when sniffing their partner was significantly lower than when sniffing a stranger (Figure 2G–I; One-Way Repeated Measures ANOVA: F (1.212, 7.274)=15.89, p=0.0039; partner vs. stranger, p=0.0366; partner vs. object, p=0.0140, stranger vs. object, p=0.0434).
evidence: Supported by fiber photometry data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2G-I.

claim: D1 MSNs activity was significantly increased relative to baseline when sniffing their partner or an unknown female after 3 days of cohabitation.
source: However, D1 MSNs activity was significantly increased relative to baseline when sniffing their partner or an unknown female after 3 days of cohabitation (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and B; A, Paired t test: partner, t (6)=2.700, p=0.0356; stranger, t (6)=2.492, p=0.0470; object, t (6)=0.5216, p=0.6207. B, Paired t test: partner, t (6)=3.591, p=0.0115; stranger, t (6)=2.381, p=0.0547; object, t (6)=1.590, p=0.1630).
evidence: Supported by fiber photometry data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and B.

claim: After 7 days of cohabitation, D1 MSNs activity significantly increased relative to baseline when sniffing their partner and was significantly higher when sniffing their partner than when sniffing an unknown female.
source: After 7 days of cohabitation, D1 MSNs activity significantly increased relative to baseline when sniffing their partner and was significantly higher when sniffing their partner than when sniffing an unknown female (Figure 3G–I; One-Way Repeated Measures ANOVA: F (1.242, 7.451)=11.11, p=0.0093; partner vs. stranger, p=0.0278, partner vs. object, p=0.0326).
evidence: Supported by fiber photometry data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3G-I.

claim: The frequency and amplitude of D2 MSNs spontaneous excitatory postsynaptic current (sEPSC) were significantly higher in paired males than in naive males.
source: The frequency and amplitude of D2 MSNs spontaneous excitatory postsynaptic current (sEPSC) were found to be significantly higher in paired males than in naive males (Figure 4B and C; Two-tailed unpaired t-test: frequency: t (20)=–3.634, p=0.002; amplitude: t (20)=–2.619, p=0.016).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recording data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: The frequency, but not the amplitude, of D2 MSNs spontaneous inhibitory postsynaptic currents (sIPSCs) was significantly increased in paired males compared to naive males.
source: In addition, the frequency, but not the amplitude, of D2 MSNs spontaneous inhibitory postsynaptic currents (sIPSCs) was significantly increased in paired males compared to naive males (Figure 4B and D) (Two-tailed unpaired t-test: frequency: t (26)=–2.096, p=0.046; amplitude: t (26)=–0.528, p=0.602).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recording data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4B and D.

claim: No significant change in intrinsic excitability in D2 MSNs was detected in both naive males and paired males.
source: However, this study failed to detect a significant change in intrinsic excitability in D2 MSNs in both naive males and paired males (Figure 4E–H) (4 F: Two-Way Repeated Measures ANOVA, group ×treatment: F (8, 198)=0.070, p=0.999; group: F (1, 198)=0.0003, p=0.986; treatment: F (8, 198)=16.767, p<0.0001; 4 G, Two-Way Repeated Measures ANOVA, group ×treatment: F (8, 198)=0.103, p=0.999; group: F (1, 198)=0.078, p=0.780; treatment: F (8, 198)=10.095, p<0.0001; 4 H, Two-tailed unpaired t-test, t (22)=0.100, p=0.921).
evidence: Supported by current-clamp recording data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4E-H.

claim: An increased E/I ratio of PSCs was found in D2 MSNs of paired males.
source: To further examine the changes in excitatory and inhibitory synaptic transmission of D2 MSNs, evoked excitatory and inhibitory postsynaptic currents (PSCs) were recorded from the same cells. An increased E/I ratio of PSCs was found in D2 MSNs of paired males (Figure 4J) (Two-tailed unpaired t-test: t (10)=–3.499, p=0.012).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recording data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4J.

claim: Bath-applied DA (5 µM) caused a significant decrease in both the frequency and amplitude of D2 sEPSC in naive males.
source: The results showed a significant decrease in both the frequency and amplitude of D2 sEPSC in naive (Figure 4K and L; Two-Way Repeated Measures ANOVA: frequencies: group ×treatment: F (1, 14)=0.0177, p=0.896; group: F (1, 14)=8.105, p=0.0129; treatment: F (1, 14)=7.189, p=0.0179, Control_ Baseline vs Control DA, p=0.0050, Cohabitation _ Baseline vs Cohabitation DA, p=0.2296, Control_ Baseline vs Cohabitation Baseline, p=0.0277, Control _DA vs Cohabitation DA, p=0.0376; amplitude: group ×treatment: F (1, 14)=0.7937, p=0.4042; group: F (1, 14)=5.911, p=0.0291; treatment: F (1, 14)=14.78, p=0.0018, Control_ Baseline vs Control DA, p=0.007, Cohabitation Baseline vs Cohabitation _DA, p=0.098, Control Baseline vs Cohabitation Baseline, p=0.0472, Control DA vs Cohabitation DA, p=0.0241), but not in paired mandarin voles (Figure 4L).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recording data with DA application and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4K and L.

claim: Bath-applied DA (5 µM) did not cause a significant change in D2 sEPSC in paired mandarin voles.
source: The results showed a significant decrease in both the frequency and amplitude of D2 sEPSC in naive (Figure 4K and L; Two-Way Repeated Measures ANOVA: frequencies: group ×treatment: F (1, 14)=0.0177, p=0.896; group: F (1, 14)=8.105, p=0.0129; treatment: F (1, 14)=7.189, p=0.0179, Control_ Baseline vs Control DA, p=0.0050, Cohabitation _ Baseline vs Cohabitation DA, p=0.2296, Control_ Baseline vs Cohabitation Baseline, p=0.0277, Control _DA vs Cohabitation DA, p=0.0376; amplitude: group ×treatment: F (1, 14)=0.7937, p=0.4042; group: F (1, 14)=5.911, p=0.0291; treatment: F (1, 14)=14.78, p=0.0018, Control_ Baseline vs Control DA, p=0.007, Cohabitation Baseline vs Cohabitation _DA, p=0.098, Control Baseline vs Cohabitation Baseline, p=0.0472, Control DA vs Cohabitation DA, p=0.0241), but not in paired mandarin voles (Figure 4L).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recording data with DA application and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4L.

claim: D1 MSNs showed reduced frequency and amplitude of sEPSC after cohabitation.
source: D1 MSNs showed reduced frequency and amplitude of sEPSC after cohabitation Figure 5B and C; (Two-tailed unpaired t-test: frequency: t (33)=2.816, p=0.008; amplitude: t (33)=3.322, p=0.002).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recording data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: In sIPSC in D1 MSNs, the frequency decreased drastically, but not the amplitude.
source: In addition, in sIPSC in D1 MSNs, the frequency decreased drastically, but not the amplitude (Figure 5B and D; Two-tailed unpaired t-test: frequency: t (24)=2.324, p=0.024; amplitude: t (24)=0.100, p=0.921).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recording data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5B and D.

claim: Differences in the E/I ratio of D1 MSNs were not found between naive and paired males.
source: differences in the E/I ratio of D1 MSNs were not found (Figure 5J; Two-tailed unpaired t-test: t (12)=–1.429, p=0.179).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recording data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5J.

claim: Bath-applied DA caused a significant increase in the frequency of D1 sEPSC in naïve males.
source: The results showed a significant increase in the frequency of D1 sEPSC in naïve males (Figure 5K and L; Two-Way Repeated Measures ANOVA: frequencies: group ×treatment: F (1, 18)=4.784, p=0.0422; group: F (1, 18)=9.954, p=0.0055; treatment: F (1, 18)=5.164, p=0.0356, Control_ Baseline vs Control DA, p=0.006, Cohabitation _ Baseline vs Cohabitation DA, p=0.953, Control Baseline vs Cohabitation _ Baseline, p=0.015, Control DA vs Cohabitation DA, p=0.006; amplitude: group ×treatment: F (1, 18)=0.007, p=0.9343; group: F (1, 18)=5.842, p=0.0265; treatment: F (1, 18)=0.6498, p=0.4307, Control_ Baseline vs Control DA, p=0.5285, Cohabitation Baseline vs Cohabitation DA, p=0.63468, Control Baseline vs Cohabitation Baseline, p=0.0282, Control DA vs Cohabitation DA, p=0.029), but not in paired males (Figure 5L).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recording data with DA application and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5K and L.

claim: Bath-applied DA did not cause a significant change in D1 sEPSC in paired males.
source: The results showed a significant increase in the frequency of D1 sEPSC in naïve males (Figure 5K and L; Two-Way Repeated Measures ANOVA: frequencies: group ×treatment: F (1, 18)=4.784, p=0.0422; group: F (1, 18)=9.954, p=0.0055; treatment: F (1, 18)=5.164, p=0.0356, Control_ Baseline vs Control DA, p=0.006, Cohabitation _ Baseline vs Cohabitation DA, p=0.953, Control Baseline vs Cohabitation _ Baseline, p=0.015, Control DA vs Cohabitation DA, p=0.006; amplitude: group ×treatment: F (1, 18)=0.007, p=0.9343; group: F (1, 18)=5.842, p=0.0265; treatment: F (1, 18)=0.6498, p=0.4307, Control_ Baseline vs Control DA, p=0.5285, Cohabitation Baseline vs Cohabitation DA, p=0.63468, Control Baseline vs Cohabitation Baseline, p=0.0282, Control DA vs Cohabitation DA, p=0.029), but not in paired males (Figure 5L).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recording data with DA application and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5L.

claim: 90.11% of mCherry cells co-expressed D2R in the chemogenetic experiment.
source: Immunohistochemical staining showed that 90.11% of mCherry cells co-expressed D2R (Figure 6B, C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 6B, C, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The addition of 10 μM CNO remarkably increased the number of action potentials in the Gq-DREADD-transfected neurons.
source: The results showed that the addition of 10 μM CNO remarkably increased the number of action potentials in the Gq-DREADD-transfected neurons (Figures 6D and 7D).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recording data shown in Figures 6D and 7D.

claim: CNO caused a significant decrease in membrane potentials in Gi-DREADD-transfected neurons.
source: In contrast, CNO caused a significant decrease in membrane potentials in Gi-DREADD-transfected neurons (Figures 6D and 7D).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recording data shown in Figures 6D and 7D.

claim: CNO-treated voles with VP-projecting D2 MSNs Gq-DREADD virus infection spent less time with their partners than with unknown females in the partner preference test after 7 days of cohabitation.
source: Nevertheless, CNO-treated voles with VP-projecting D2 MSNs Gq-DREADD virus infection spent less time with their partners than with unknown females in the partner preference test; moreover, such activation of VP-projecting D2 MSNs also blocked partner preference after 7 days of cohabitation (Figure 6I and J; 6I, Two-way ANOVA: group ×treatment: F (2, 40)=3.798, p=0.031; group: F (2, 40)=6.797, p=0.003; treatment: F (1, 40)=3.375, p=0.074; Gi_Saline vs Gi_CNO, p=0.861; Gq_Saline vs Gq_CNO, p=0.002; mCherry_Saline vs mCherry_CNO, p=0.805. 6 J, Kruskal-Wallis: H=8.083, p=0.044; CNO_Partner vs CNO_Stranger, p=0.384; saline_Partner vs saline_Stranger, p=0.033).
evidence: Supported by partner preference test data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 6I and J.

claim: Activation of VP-projecting D2 MSNs blocked partner preference after 7 days of cohabitation.
source: Nevertheless, CNO-treated voles with VP-projecting D2 MSNs Gq-DREADD virus infection spent less time with their partners than with unknown females in the partner preference test; moreover, such activation of VP-projecting D2 MSNs also blocked partner preference after 7 days of cohabitation (Figure 6I and J; 6I, Two-way ANOVA: group ×treatment: F (2, 40)=3.798, p=0.031; group: F (2, 40)=6.797, p=0.003; treatment: F (1, 40)=3.375, p=0.074; Gi_Saline vs Gi_CNO, p=0.861; Gq_Saline vs Gq_CNO, p=0.002; mCherry_Saline vs mCherry_CNO, p=0.805. 6 J, Kruskal-Wallis: H=8.083, p=0.044; CNO_Partner vs CNO_Stranger, p=0.384; saline_Partner vs saline_Stranger, p=0.033).
evidence: Supported by partner preference test data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 6I and J.

claim: In control virus subjects, CNO had no detectable effects on the behavioral performance in tests.
source: In control virus subjects, CNO had no detectable effects on the behavioral performance in tests (Figure 6L); (Two-Way Repeated Measures ANOVA: group ×treatment: F (1, 11)=0.043, p=0.839; group: F (1, 11)=0.306, p=0.591; treatment: F (1, 11)=25.166, p=0.0004; CNO_Partner vs CNO_Stranger, p=0.009; saline_Partner vs saline_Stranger, p=0.009).
evidence: Supported by control experiment data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 6L.

claim: CNO-treated voles with VP-projecting D1 MSNs Gi-DREADD virus infection showed trends to reduce side-by-side contact with their partners compared to saline-treated voles in the partner preference test after 7 days of cohabitation.
source: In the partner preference test, CNO-treated voles with VP-projecting D1 MSNs Gi-DREADD virus infection showed trends to reduce side-by-side contact with their partners compared to saline-treated voles in the partner preference test after 7 days of cohabitation (Figure 7E, G, I and K; 7E, Two-way ANOVA: group ×treatment: F (2, 37)=0.186, p=0.831; group: F (2, 37)=2.729, p=0.078; treatment: F (1, 37)=2.839, p=0.100. 7 G, Kruskal-Wallis: H=9.597, p=0.022; CNO_Partner vs CNO_Stranger, p=0.087; saline_Partner vs saline_Stranger, p=0.821. 7I, Two-way ANOVA: group ×treatment: F (2, 37)=4.934, p=0.013; group: F (2, 37)=0.873, p=0.426; treatment: F (1, 37)=7.633, p=0.009; Gq_Saline vs Gq_CNO, p=0.001; Gi_Saline vs Gi_CNO, p=0.109; mCherry_Saline vs mCherry_CNO, P=0.522. 7 K, Two-Way Repeated Measures ANOVA: group ×treatment: F (1, 11)=4.281, p=0.063; group: F (1, 11)=1.513, p=0.244; treatment: F (1, 11)=11.027, p=0.007; CNO_Partner vs CNO_Stranger, p=0.377; saline_Partner vs saline_Stranger, p=0.004).
evidence: Supported by partner preference test data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 7E, G, I and K.

claim: CNO-treated voles with VP-projecting D1 MSNs Gq-DREADD virus infection showed a significant reduction in side-by-side time spent with their partner than saline-treated voles in the partner preference test after 7 days of cohabitation and showed no partner preference.
source: In addition, CNO-treated voles with VP-projecting D1 MSNs Gq-DREADD virus infection showed a significant reduction in side-by-side time spent with their partner than saline-treated voles in the partner preference test after 7 days of cohabitation and showed no partner preference (Figure 7E, F, I and J) (7 F, Kruskal-Wallis: H=0.743, p=0.863. 7 J, Kruskal-Wallis: H=12.819, p=0.005; CNO_Partner vs CNO_Stranger, p=0.256; saline_Partner vs saline_Stranger, p=0.001).
evidence: Supported by partner preference test data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 7E, F, I and J.

claim: Different neuronal activity of NAc shell D1 MSNs / D2 MSNs regulated by increasing DA release after pair bonding may be a neurobiological mechanism underlying pair bond formation.
source: These findings suggest that different neuronal activity of NAc shell D1 MSNs / D2 MSNs regulated by increasing DA release after pair bonding may be a neurobiological mechanism underlying pair bond formation.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the combined experimental findings from the study.

claim: The level of real-time DA release in voles may be different depending on whether they encounter their own partner or an unfamiliar vole of the opposite sex.
source: Because DA plays an important role in behaviors associated with reward, behavioral reinforcement, and addiction (Perra et al., 2011), we predict that the level of real-time DA release in voles may be different depending on whether they encounter their own partner or an unfamiliar vole of the opposite sex.
evidence: This is a prediction based on established knowledge about DA function and the experimental design.

claim: DA binding with D2R is coupled with Gi and produces an inhibitory effect.
source: DA binding with D2R is coupled with Gi and produces an inhibitory effect (Lobo and Nestler, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research (Lobo and Nestler, 2011).

claim: It is generally assumed that the activation of D2R produces aversive and negative reinforcement.
source: It is generally assumed that the activation of D2R produces aversive and negative reinforcement.
evidence: This is stated as a general assumption in the field.

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of NAc D2 MSNs is sufficient to enhance reward-oriented motivation in motivational tasks.
source: Our results also align with other previous studies, which showed that chemogenetic inhibition of NAc D2 MSNs is sufficient to enhance reward-oriented motivation in motivational tasks (Carvalho Poyraz et al., 2016; Gallo et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research (Carvalho Poyraz et al., 2016; Gallo et al., 2018).

evidence: Supported by citation to previous research (Bock et al., 2013).

evidence: Supported by citation to previous research (Lobo and Nestler, 2011).

claim: The activation of D1R produces reward and positive reinforcement.

evidence: Supported by citations to previous research (Hikida et al., 2010; Kwak and Jung, 2019; Tai et al., 2012).

source: For example, activation of D1 MSNs enhances the cocaine-induced conditioned place preference (Lobo et al., 2010).

evidence: Supported by citation to previous research (Liu et al., 2022).

source: One possible explanation is that almost all D1 MSNs projecting to the VTA/substantia nigra (SN) send collaterals to the VP (Pardo-Garcia et al., 2019).

source: This indicates that D2R is crucial for the initial formation of the pair bond.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited experimental result and the discussion context.

source: Secondly, it is important to further examine whether other neural circuits also influence the formation of partner preference, such as basolateral amygdala projections to NAc. Moreover, in general, natal philopatry among mammals is female-biased in the wild (Brody and Armitage, 1985; Greenwood, 1983; Ims, 1990; Solomon and Jacquot, 2002).
